title: The Carmelites of Compiègne (1794)
hook: sixteen nuns go to the guillotine singing during the French Revolution

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lorenzo Ricci and the Jesuits: dissolved under pressure from kings, kept alive in Russia, then restored. Your line was restored. Today, the Revolution comes for a convent.

Singing rises over the noise of a Paris crowd. Carts roll toward the guillotine in this season of the Revolution. The crowd is used to shouting, to jeering, to fear. But the women in these carts are singing Latin hymns, the way they sang them in their chapel. Tradition says the crowd grew quiet. These are Carmelite nuns from the town of Compiègne, north of Paris. Their convent was closed. Their habits were taken. They are going to their deaths, and they are singing.
screen: `CARTS TOWARD THE GUILLOTINE.` → `THE WOMEN ARE SINGING.` → `THE CROWD GROWS QUIET.`

segments.voice: First, the closed convent. The revolutionary government shut down religious houses, and the Carmelites of Compiègne were turned out. They split into small groups in town, wore ordinary clothes, and kept praying their hours together as best they could. Second, the offering. Before the danger came close, their prioress, Mother Teresa of Saint Augustine, proposed that the community offer themselves to God for peace, for France and for the Church. Tradition says some sisters were afraid at first. In the end, they joined. Third, the trial. They were arrested, taken to Paris and brought before the Revolutionary Tribunal. Among the charges was fanaticism. Tradition says one sister asked what the word meant, was told it meant attachment to their religion, and was glad to be condemned for that. Fourth, the scaffold. Tradition says they sang the Veni Creator on the way, and at the foot of the scaffold each sister knelt before the prioress, renewed her vows, and climbed, while those still waiting sang on. The prioress went last. One of the songs tradition gives them is a short psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "O praise the Lord, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people." The Church later declared them blessed, and Pope Francis declared them saints. Their story was retold in a play by Georges Bernanos and an opera by Francis Poulenc, Dialogues of the Carmelites. But before any stage, there was a real cart, real voices, and a hymn that didn't stop.
screen: `A CONVENT CLOSED.` · `AN OFFERING FOR PEACE.` · `CONDEMNED FOR FANATICISM.` · `ONE BY ONE, SINGING.` · then, large: `O PRAISE THE LORD, ALL YE NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something hard in front of you, a conversation, a test, a diagnosis, a long day, and hum or sing very quietly one line of a song or hymn you know by heart: not a performance, just a voice held steady. Notice what happens to your breathing as you sing. If you pray, sing the psalm's line the Carmelites sang; if not, any steady song will do.
Laudate Dominum. Praise the Lord, the opening of the psalm tradition says the Carmelites of Compiègne sang on their way to the guillotine.
Your line: singing to the scaffold. They sang on the cart the hymns they had sung in their chapel. Day eight hundred seventy-three, done.

howItsDone: Carmelite communities and other Catholics remember the martyrs of Compiègne on their feast day, and performances of Poulenc's Dialogues of the Carmelites keep their story before audiences far beyond the Church.

chat.says: What were the Carmelite nuns singing on the way to the guillotine?
options: Tradition says hymns: the Veni Creator, and Laudate Dominum, praise the Lord.
A revolutionary song, to show the crowd they were loyal to France.
Nothing at all; tradition says they went in silence, as their rule asked.
chat.meaning: Tradition gives them the Veni Creator and a short psalm, Laudate Dominum: O praise the Lord, all ye nations.

notes: Claims rule: the number of nuns (sixteen, in the index hook) and the date are not spoken. Confirm.
Prioress: Mother Teresa of Saint Augustine (Madeleine Lidoine). The offering ('act of consecration' for peace) and initial fear of some sisters attributed to tradition; confirm.
The 'fanaticism' exchange is attributed to tradition (Sister Henriette of Jesus is the sister usually named); confirm.
Hymns: Veni Creator and Laudate Dominum (Psalm 116/117) are the commonly reported songs, along with the Salve Regina and Te Deum in some accounts; given as tradition.
Beatified (1906) and canonized by Pope Francis (equipollent canonization, 2024): stated without dates. Confirm.
Psalm numbering follows the Vulgate as in Douay-Rheims; confirm the citation format.
